cards.title: 1.1.1 Measuring the Rate of a Chemical Reaction
body: The phrase “rate of reaction” means how fast the reaction is occurring or the speed of the reaction.

The rate of a reaction can be measured either in terms of how much of a reactant is being used up per unit of time or in terms of how much of a product is being formed per unit of time, depending on which is easier to do as the reaction proceeds.
The rate will then be measured by reading the volume of gas collected per unit of time.
The rate of a given reaction is not always the same.

body: A chemical reaction may be either reversible or irreversible.

cards.title: The law of mass action, step by step
body: **Law of mass action** (Guldberg and Waage, 1864): at constant temperature, the rate of a reaction is proportional to the product of the molar concentrations of the reactants, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation.
**Step 1 — Write both rates** for \(a\text{A} + b\text{B} \rightleftharpoons c\text{C} + d\text{D}\):
$$\text{rate}_f = k_f[\text{A}]^a[\text{B}]^b \qquad \text{rate}_b = k_b[\text{C}]^c[\text{D}]^d$$
**Step 2 — At equilibrium the two rates are equal:** \(k_f[\text{A}]^a[\text{B}]^b = k_b[\text{C}]^c[\text{D}]^d\).
**Step 3 — Collect the constants on one side:**
$$K_c = \frac{k_f}{k_b} = \frac{[\text{C}]^c[\text{D}]^d}{[\text{A}]^a[\text{B}]^b}$$

**Rules for writing Kc:** products on top, reactants below; each concentration (in mol/L) raised to its coefficient; concentrations are the **equilibrium** values. For gases you may use partial pressures instead → **Kp**. Pure solids and pure liquids are left out (their “concentration” is constant).
**Kc changes only with temperature** — not with concentration, pressure or a catalyst.
**Size of K:** K ≫ 1 → mostly products at equilibrium; K ≪ 1 → mostly reactants; K ≈ 1 → appreciable amounts of both.

cards.title: Reaction quotient Q: which way will it go?
body: Q is calculated exactly like K but with the concentrations **at any moment** (not necessarily at equilibrium). Compare Q with K:
**Q < K** → too little product → net reaction goes **forward (to the right)**.
**Q = K** → at equilibrium → no net change.
**Q > K** → too much product → net reaction goes **backward (to the left)**.

cards.title: Le Chatelier’s principle, step by step
body: **Le Chatelier’s principle:** if a stress is applied to a system at equilibrium, the system shifts so as to **reduce (oppose) the stress** and reaches a new equilibrium position.
**Step 1 — Name the stress:** more or less of a substance (concentration), higher or lower pressure (volume), higher or lower temperature.
**Step 2 — Ask how the system can undo it:** use up what was added; replace what was removed; reduce a pressure increase by making fewer gas molecules.
**Step 3 — State the direction:** “shifts to the right (forward)” or “to the left (backward)”.
**Step 4 — State the result:** what happens to the amount of each substance, the colour, the yield.
**Concentration:** add a reactant or remove a product → shifts **right**; add a product or remove a reactant → shifts **left**. Kc does **not** change.

**Pressure (gases only):** count the **moles of gas** on each side. Increase pressure (decrease volume) → shift to the side with **fewer** gas moles; decrease pressure → side with **more** gas moles. Equal gas moles on both sides → **no shift**. Kc does not change.

**Also remember:** raising the temperature shifts an equilibrium in the **endothermic** direction (this *does* change K); a catalyst does **not** shift the equilibrium — it only helps reach it faster.

cards.problem: Show with Q why halving the volume of an equilibrium mixture of N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ shifts it to the right.

steps.text: At equilibrium \(Q = K = \dfrac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3}\).
Halving the volume **doubles** every concentration at that instant.
Q < K → the reaction goes forward (right) until Q rises back to K — more NH₃, fewer gas molecules, lower pressure.

steps.text: (a) A reactant is added → the system uses it up → shifts **right**; more HI, less I₂ (the purple colour fades).
(b) 2 gas moles on each side → **no shift** (pressure has no effect).
(c) A reactant is removed → the system replaces it → shifts **left**; SO₃ decomposes.
(d) Lower pressure → side with **more** gas moles (1 → 2) → shifts **right**; more PCl₃ and Cl₂.

cards.title: Tips and common mistakes
body: Concentration and pressure changes move the **position**, not the **value** of K. Only temperature changes K.
Count only **gas** moles for pressure questions.

cards.title: Reversible reactions and equilibrium
body: A **reversible reaction** can go both ways (⇌). In a closed system it reaches **dynamic equilibrium**: the forward and reverse rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant, though both reactions are still going on.

**Le Chatelier’s principle:** if a change is made to a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. Example, the Haber process N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic forward reaction): increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right (fewer gas molecules, 4 → 2), so more ammonia forms; increasing the temperature shifts it to the left, so less ammonia forms.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the effect of pressure.**
Pressure affects equilibrium only if there is a change in the total number of moles of gas between reactants and products.

**Step 2: Count gas moles.**

**Result:** Since the number of moles is equal on both sides ($$ 2 = 2 $$), changing the pressure has no effect on the equilibrium position.

tips.text: Rate or speed refers to the amount of change in something per unit of time.
In a chemical reaction the quantity changing is the concentration of reactants and products or a certain physical property that is related to one of the concentrations.
The rate of reaction can be expressed in terms of the rate of change in concentration of either the reactants or the products.
Two conditions we impose on the reaction rate are that it must be a positive quantity, and that it must be of the same quantity regardless of the substance we use to express it.
A rate law (equation) shows us how the rate of a reaction varies with reactant concentration. But chemists also need an equation to show how reactant concentration changes with time.
This equation would allow us to summarize experimental data, which are usually reactant concentrations versus time.
We can also answer such questions as, how long will it take for a reaction to be 50 per cent complete, or what will the reactant concentration be after 5 hours.

The rate constant’s dependence on temperature can be explained by the collision theory. This theory assumes that, for a reaction to occur, reactant molecules must collide with an energy greater than a certain minimum value and with the proper orientation.
This minimum energy required for a collision between two reactant molecules, causing them to react, is called the activation energy, EA.

Some of the main factors that affect the rate of a reaction are: the temperature, the size of the particles of a solid reactant, the concentration of reactants in a solution, the pressure of reactants in the gas phase, the nature of the reactants and the presence or absence of catalyst.

questions.q:
Ammonia gas can be prepared in the Haber process from nitrogen and hydrogen gas as follows:
$$ N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g) \quad \Delta H = -92 \text{ KJ/mole} $$
Then large amount of ammonia is produced by:

options.A: Decreasing the temperature of the reactant
options.B: Increasing pressure on the reacting substance
options.C: Continuous addition of nitrogen gas and hydrogen gas

why:
According to **Le Chatelier's Principle**:
1. Since the reaction is **exothermic** ($$ \Delta H $$ is negative), decreasing temperature (A) shifts the equilibrium to the right.
2. Increasing pressure (B) shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer gas moles (the product side).
3. Adding more reactants (C) shifts the equilibrium to the right.
Therefore, A, B, and C all increase ammonia production.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: In the reaction $$ N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightarrow 2NH_3(g) $$. The increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium state to
why:
**Step 1:** Count the number of moles of gas on each side of the equation.
- Reactants: $$ 1 (N_2) + 3 (H_2) = 4 $$ moles of gas.
- Products: $$ 2 (NH_3) = 2 $$ moles of gas.

**Step 2:** Apply Le Chatelier's Principle.
- An increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the side with the **fewer** number of gas moles to reduce the pressure.
- Since 2 is less than 4, the equilibrium shifts to the **Right**.

**Result:** B
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The following parameters increase the rate of a reaction by increasing the rate of collision, **except**:
why:
**Step 1: Analyze how each factor affects the reaction rate.**
- **Temperature:** Increases kinetic energy, leading to more frequent and energetic collisions.
- **Concentration:** More particles in a given volume increase collision frequency.
- **Surface Area:** More exposed particles increase collision frequency.
- **Pressure:** For gases, increases particle density, increasing collision frequency.
- **Catalyst:** Increases the rate by providing an alternative pathway with a **lower activation energy**, not by increasing the collision frequency.

**Result:** Catalyst is the exception.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: For a reaction $$ A + B \leftrightarrow C + \text{heat} $$, increase in temperature will increase
why:
According to **Le Chatelier's Principle**, if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to counteract the disturbance.
- The reaction is **exothermic** (heat is a product).
- Adding heat (increasing temperature) will shift the equilibrium to the **left** (the endothermic direction) to absorb the excess heat.
- Shifting left means the **backward reaction** is favored.

**Result:** B
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: For a reaction $$ \text{A} + \text{B} \leftrightarrow \text{C} + \text{heat} $$, increase in temperature will increase
why: According to Le Chatelier's Principle, for an **exothermic** reaction (where heat is a product), increasing the temperature is like adding more product. The system will shift to the left to consume the excess heat, thereby increasing the **backward reaction**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: According to the collision theory, rate of a reaction decreases when ____.
why:
According to **Collision Theory**, the rate of reaction is proportional to the frequency of effective collisions. 
- Increasing pressure, surface area, concentration, or temperature all **increase** the rate. 
- Increasing **particle size** (e.g., using a large lump instead of powder) **decreases** the surface area, which leads to fewer collisions and a **decreased** reaction rate.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Consider the reaction: $$ 2H_{2(g)} + O_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2H_2O_{(g)} \quad \Delta H = -483.6 kJ $$. Which of the following is true about the reaction?

options.A: Increasing temperature will shift the equilibrium to the left.
options.B: Increasing pressure will shift the equilibrium to the left.
options.C: Increasing Volume will not have any effect on the equilibrium.
options.D: Increasing concentration of O2(g) will shift the equilibrium to the left

why:
**Step 1: Temperature.** The reaction is exothermic ($$ \Delta H < 0 $$). According to Le Chatelier's Principle, increasing temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the endothermic direction (left). (True)
**Step 2: Pressure.** Reactant moles = 3, Product moles = 2. Increasing pressure shifts to the side with fewer moles (right). (False)
**Step 3: Concentration.** Increasing $$ O_2 $$ (reactant) shifts equilibrium to the product side (right). (False).
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: The rate of reaction is increased by the following, except;

options.C: Increasing the size of the particle

why:
**Step 1:** Review factors that increase reaction rate.
- **Temp:** Increases kinetic energy and collisions (Increases rate).
- **Conc:** More particles per volume, more collisions (Increases rate).
- **Catalyst:** Lowers activation energy (Increases rate).
- **Surface Area:** More area for collisions (Increases rate).
**Step 2:** **Increasing particle size** actually **decreases** the surface area. Therefore, it **decreases** the rate of reaction.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: For the decomposition of $$ SO_3 $$ to form $$ SO_2 $$ and $$ O_2 $$, $$ K_c $$ is $$ 2.43 \times 10^{-3} $$ at $$ 273 ^\circ\text{C} $$. Then what is the $$ K_c $$ for the **reverse reaction**?
why:
The equilibrium constant for a reverse reaction ($$ K' $$) is the reciprocal of the equilibrium constant for the forward reaction ($$ K $$).
$$ K' = 1 / K $$
$$ K' = 1 / (2.43 \times 10^{-3}) $$
$$ K' \approx 411.52 \approx 4.12 \times 10^2 $$.

A catalyst increases the rate. **Light** does not significantly affect this specific gaseous reaction.

**Step 2: Determine which ion migrates to the negative cathode**
Cations (positively charged) migrate to the negative cathode. Thus, $$Pb^{2+}$$ migrates to the cathode.

**Step 3: Determine the reaction at the cathode**
At the cathode, reduction occurs: $$Pb^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Pb(s)$$.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the oxidation number of sulfur ($$S$$) in sulfuric acid ($$H_2SO_4$$)?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Assign known oxidation numbers**
Hydrogen is assigned $$+1$$ and oxygen is assigned $$-2$$.

**Step 2: Setup the algebraic sum for a neutral compound**
The sum of the oxidation numbers in a neutral molecule must equal zero.
$$2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0$$

**Step 3: Solve for $$x$$**
$$2 + x - 8 = 0 \implies x - 6 = 0 \implies x = +6$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The oxidation number of sulfur in $$H_2SO_4$$ is **$$+6$$**.

cards.title: 2.2.1 What is Electrolysis?
body: **Electrolysis** is the process in which electrical energy is used to cause a non-spontaneous chemical reaction to occur.
**An electrolytic cell** is an apparatus for carrying out electrolysis.
The electrolytic cell consists of an electrolyte, electrodes and a source of electricity.
The electric source for electrolysis should be a direct current (DC) or small batteries (e.g., a few 1.5V cells in series).

cards.title: 2.2.2 The Mechanism of Electrolysis
body: The conduction of electricity through an electrolyte (either molten or aqueous state) is due to the migration of the ions towards their oppositely charged electrodes.
During the electrolysis, a battery or other DC sources move electrons through the wire to the electrodes.
The electrons enter the electrolyte through the cathode; positively charged ions (cations) move to the negative electrode (cathode) and thus receive electrons and are reduced.
After electrolysis, at both electrodes, the ions are converted into neutral atoms Therefore, there is a transfer of electrons between the electrodes and the ions.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Electrolysis of Molten Electrolytes
body: Lead bromide can be used to demonstrate the electrolysis of molten electrolytes because it has fairly lower melting point.
Decomposition of the electrolyte into its ions by heat.
Discharge of the ions into their respective neutral substances at the surface of the electrodes, that is, reduction takes place at the cathode.
The atoms of lead are deposited at the surface of cathode with characteristic grayish color.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions of Electrolytes
body: In the electrolysis of aqueous solutions, it is not only the electrolyte that dissociates but water also dissociates partially.
For example, in the electrolysis of aqueous solution of NaCl four ions exist in solution, that is, two ions (Na+ and Cl-) from sodium chloride and two ions from the water ( H+ and OH-).
\eeping the other factors constant, if two different ions are present at the surface of the cathode, the one which readily receives electrons is preferentially discharged.
For example, if both sodium and hydrogen ions are present on the surface of the electrode, H+ is preferentially discharged to Na+.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Applications of Electrolysis
body: Material required: 1 beaker, 2 carbon rods, 25 g Copper (II) chloride, 150mL water, teaspoon, 6 V battery, 2 wires.

Add three teaspoons of copper(II) chloride to the beaker.
Stir the solution until all of the copper(II) chloride dissolves.

cards.title: 2.2.6 Faraday’s Law of Electrolysis
body: The quantitative relationship between the amount of electricity passed through an electrolytes solution and the extent of the product is given by Faraday’s laws.
Faraday’s First Law of Electrolysis states that the mass of a substance produced by electrolysis is proportional to the quantity of electricity used.

Faraday's second law states that the mass of two substances that are deposited or liberated from electrodes, given the same applied electrical charge, is directly proportional to the equivalent masses of the two substances.

cards.title: 3.2.1 Carbon
body: Carbon is found in all living things, both plants and animals.
Carbon occurs both in a free and in a combined state.

In its combined state carbon exists as carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, carbonates such as calcium carbonate, and in large quantities as organic compounds, such as hydrocarbons, oils, carbohydrates and proteins.
Allotropes are different forms of the same element that have different physical properties, but generally have the same chemical properties.

cards.title: The allotropes of carbon, step by step
body: **Allotropes** are different forms of the same element in the same physical state, with different structures and so different physical properties, but the same chemical properties (all three burn to CO₂). Carbon has three main crystalline allotropes: **diamond, graphite and fullerene**; charcoal, soot and coke are amorphous forms.

**Diamond:** every carbon atom forms **4 strong covalent bonds** to 4 other carbons arranged **tetrahedrally** (109.5°). The bonding continues in all directions → a **giant 3-D covalent network**. All 4 outer electrons are used in bonds.

**Graphite:** every carbon forms **3 covalent bonds** in a flat sheet of **hexagons** (120°). The 4th electron of each atom is **delocalised** (free to move along the sheet). The sheets (layers) are held together only by **weak forces**, so they slide over each other.

**Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀:** discovered in 1985. 60 carbon atoms form a hollow ball of **12 pentagons and 20 hexagons**, like a football (“buckyball”). Each C bonds to 3 others. It is a **molecule**, not a giant structure — so it is much softer and dissolves in some organic solvents (e.g. benzene, giving a purple solution).

cards.title: Diamond: giant 3-D network
body: Every atom is joined to four others. There are no weak links and no free electrons.

cards.title: Graphite: layers of hexagons
body: Strong bonds inside each layer, weak forces between the layers.

cards.title: Buckminsterfullerene, C₆₀
body: A closed cage of 60 atoms: 12 pentagons (one is shaded) surrounded by hexagons.

head: Property
Diamond
Graphite

cards.title: Structure → property: the reasoning chain
body: **Hardness:** diamond has strong bonds in every direction → nothing can slide → very hard. Graphite’s layers are joined only by weak forces → layers slide → soft and slippery.
**Conductivity:** graphite has a delocalised electron on every atom that can move along the layers → conducts. Diamond’s electrons are all locked in bonds → insulator.
**Melting point:** to melt diamond or graphite you must break strong **covalent** bonds → both very high. C₆₀ molecules are held by weak forces between molecules → much lower.
Use this chain in every “explain” question: **structure → bonding → property**.

cards.title: Worked example: why does graphite conduct but diamond does not?
cards.problem: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not, although both are pure carbon.

steps.text: Electricity needs charged particles that can move.
Diamond: each C uses all 4 outer electrons in 4 covalent bonds → no free electrons → non-conductor.
Graphite: each C uses only 3 electrons in bonds; the 4th is delocalised along the layer.
These delocalised electrons move when a voltage is applied → graphite conducts (along the layers).

cards.answer: Graphite has delocalised electrons; diamond has none.

cards.title: Worked example: high melting point but soft?
cards.problem: Graphite has a higher melting point than diamond but is very soft. How can both be true?

steps.text: Melting graphite means breaking the strong covalent bonds **within** the layers → very high melting point.
Softness depends on the **weak forces between** the layers, which let the layers slide (pencil marks, lubricant).
So different forces control the two properties.

cards.answer: Strong bonds inside layers (high m.p.); weak forces between layers (soft).

cards.title: Memory trick
body: **Diamond = 4 = Fixed** (all electrons in bonds: hard, no current). **Graphite = 3 + 1 free** (layers slide, electrons flow). **C₆₀ = football** (12 pentagons + 20 hexagons).

cards.title: Carbonic acid, step by step
body: **Formation:** carbon dioxide dissolves slightly in water and some of it reacts: CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq). Carbonic acid exists **only in solution**; it is **weak** and **unstable** — warming or opening a soft-drink bottle drives the CO₂ out.
**Weak acid:** only a small fraction ionises, so it turns blue litmus red **slowly** and only faintly.
**Dibasic (diprotic):** it has two replaceable H and ionises in two steps:
$$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{HCO}_3^- \qquad \text{HCO}_3^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{CO}_3^{2-}$$
**Two series of salts:** **hydrogen carbonates** (acid salts, HCO₃⁻), e.g. NaHCO₃, and **carbonates** (normal salts, CO₃²⁻), e.g. Na₂CO₃, CaCO₃.

**Solubility and heat:** Na and K carbonates dissolve in water and are **not** decomposed by heat. Carbonates of Ca, Mg, Zn, Cu … are insoluble and decompose on heating: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). Hydrogen carbonates decompose easily: 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(g) + CO₂(g) (why baking soda makes dough rise).

**Everyday links:** soda water and soft drinks; normal rain is slightly acidic (pH ≈ 5.6) because of dissolved CO₂; rain with CO₂ slowly dissolves limestone: CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → Ca(HCO₃)₂ (caves, temporary hardness of water).

cards.title: Worked example: CO₂ into sodium hydroxide
cards.problem: Carbon dioxide is bubbled into sodium hydroxide solution, first a little, then in excess. Write the equations.

steps.text: Little CO₂ (NaOH in excess) → the normal salt: 2NaOH + CO₂ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O
Excess CO₂ → the acid salt: Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → 2NaHCO₃
Overall with excess CO₂: NaOH + CO₂ → NaHCO₃

cards.answer: Na₂CO₃ first, then NaHCO₃ with excess CO₂ — two salts because H₂CO₃ is dibasic.

cards.title: Worked example: the limewater test
cards.problem: Explain why limewater turns milky with CO₂ and then clears again if CO₂ is bubbled for a long time.

steps.text: Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution.
CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O: insoluble white CaCO₃ makes it **milky**.
Excess CO₂: CaCO₃ + H₂O + CO₂ → Ca(HCO₃)₂, which is **soluble** → the solution clears.

cards.title: Step by step: Sulphur and its compounds
body: **Step 1:** Sulphur is a yellow, brittle non-metal, insoluble in water but soluble in carbon disulphide; it has allotropes (rhombic, stable below 96 °C, and monoclinic).
**Step 2:** It burns with a blue flame to form sulphur dioxide: S + O₂ → SO₂.

**Step 3:** In the laboratory SO₂ is made from sodium sulphite and dilute HCl: Na₂SO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + SO₂; it is a dense gas collected by downward delivery. SO₂ is acidic and a bleaching/reducing agent.

**Step 4:** Contact process: (1) burn S → SO₂; (2) 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ over V₂O₅ catalyst at about 450 °C and 1–2 atm; (3) absorb SO₃ in concentrated H₂SO₄ to form oleum H₂S₂O₇; (4) dilute: H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄.
**Step 5:** Concentrated H₂SO₄ is a dehydrating agent (chars sugar), an oxidising agent and a strong acid when dilute; uses include fertilizers, batteries and detergents.

**Example:** Why not dissolve SO₃ directly in water? The reaction is so exothermic that it forms a fine acid mist that is hard to collect, so SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ first, then diluted.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Burn, Catalyse, Absorb, Dilute"

cards.title: The activity series, step by step
body: The **activity (reactivity) series** lists metals from the **most reactive** (top) to the **least reactive** (bottom). Hydrogen (and often carbon) is included as a reference.
**Why the order?** Metals react by **losing electrons** to form positive ions. The easier a metal loses electrons, the higher it is in the series.
**How it is found:** compare how vigorously metals react with **oxygen, water and dilute acids** (textbook Activity on p.120), and which metal **displaces** which from solutions of their salts.
**The textbook series (Table 4.1):** K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > (H) > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au. (Sn sits between Fe and Pb; Pt below Au.)

cards.title: Model: what the position tells you

steps.text: **Water:** K, Na, Ca react with cold water (→ hydroxide + H₂); Mg (hot water/steam), Al, Zn, Fe react with steam (→ oxide + H₂); metals below Fe do not react.
**Dilute acids:** metals **above hydrogen** displace H₂ from dilute HCl or H₂SO₄; metals **below hydrogen** (Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, Pt) do not.
**Extraction:** the higher the metal, the harder it is to extract: electrolysis for K → Al, reduction with carbon for Zn → Cu, and Ag, Au, Pt are found native.

cards.title: Uses of the activity series
body: **1. Predict reactions with water and acids** (table above) — e.g. why we never put sodium in acid, why copper vessels do not react with vinegar.

**2. Predict displacement reactions:** a metal displaces any metal **below** it from a solution of its salt. Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s) (blue colour fades, red-brown copper forms). Cu + ZnSO₄ → **no reaction**. Cu(s) + 2AgNO₃(aq) → Cu(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2Ag(s).

**3. Choose the extraction method:** metals above carbon (K → Al) need **electrolysis**; metals below carbon (Zn → Cu) can be **reduced with carbon or CO**; the least reactive (Ag, Au, Pt) occur **native** — that is why gold was the first metal people used.

**4. Protect iron from rusting:** a more reactive metal corrodes **instead of** iron — zinc coating (**galvanising**) on roofing sheets, magnesium or zinc blocks bolted to ship hulls and buried pipes (**sacrificial protection**).
**5. Predict stability of compounds:** compounds of metals high in the series are hard to decompose (Na₂CO₃ is stable to heat; CuCO₃ decomposes easily).
**6. Choose containers:** do not store copper(II) sulfate solution in an iron or zinc container — the container would be eaten away (Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu).

cards.problem: Predict whether a reaction occurs and write the equation: (a) Fe + CuSO₄(aq); (b) Cu + FeSO₄(aq); (c) Mg + ZnCl₂(aq); (d) Ag + HCl(aq).

steps.text: (a) Fe is above Cu → **yes**: Fe(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + Cu(s) (iron nail turns copper-coloured, blue fades).
(b) Cu is below Fe → **no reaction**.
(c) Mg is above Zn → **yes**: Mg(s) + ZnCl₂(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + Zn(s).
(d) Ag is below H → **no reaction** (no H₂).

cards.title: Worked example: placing an unknown metal
cards.problem: Metal X reacts with dilute HCl to give H₂ but does not react with cold water. X displaces copper from CuSO₄ solution but does not displace zinc from ZnSO₄. Where is X in the series? Suggest what X could be.

steps.text: Reacts with dilute acid → X is **above H**.
No reaction with cold water → X is **below Ca** (and Mg reacts with hot water).
Displaces Cu → X is **above Cu**; does not displace Zn → X is **below Zn**.
So X lies between Zn and H: **Fe, Sn or Pb** (iron is the usual answer).

cards.answer: Between Zn and H — for example iron.

cards.title: Worked example: choosing an extraction method
cards.problem: Suggest how each metal is obtained from its ore and why: aluminium, iron, gold.

steps.text: Aluminium is above carbon → carbon cannot remove oxygen from Al₂O₃ → **electrolysis** of molten Al₂O₃ (dissolved in cryolite).
Iron is below carbon → **reduction with carbon monoxide** in a blast furnace: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.
Gold is very unreactive → found **native**; it only needs to be separated from rock (e.g. at Bisha in Eritrea).

cards.answer: Al: electrolysis; Fe: reduction by CO/C; Au: native.

**Tip:** The same free electrons explain why metals conduct heat well and are shiny.

cards.title: Worked: metal displacement
cards.problem: Will Zn metal displace Cu²⁺ from CuSO₄(aq)? (Zn is above Cu in the activity series.)

steps.text: A more active metal reduces ions of a less active metal.
Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Net: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.

cards.answer: Yes — copper metal plates out; the blue Cu²⁺ colour fades.

cards.title: 4.2 Sodium and its compounds
body: **Occurrence:** sodium is too reactive to occur free. Its main source is **rock salt / sea water (NaCl)**; other minerals include Chile saltpetre (NaNO₃), borax and soda ash (Na₂CO₃).

**Extraction — Downs cell:** molten NaCl (mixed with CaCl₂ to lower the melting point from about 801 °C to about 600 °C) is electrolysed. Cathode (iron): Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (liquid sodium floats up and is collected). Anode (graphite): 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. A steel gauze keeps Na and Cl₂ apart so they do not recombine.

**Properties:** soft silvery metal (cut with a knife), low density (floats on water), low melting point (98 °C), one valence electron → forms Na⁺. Stored under paraffin oil because it reacts with air and water. Burns with a **yellow flame** forming Na₂O / Na₂O₂.

**Important compounds:** NaOH (caustic soda — soap, paper, made by electrolysis of brine); Na₂CO₃ (washing soda — glass, softening hard water, made by the Solvay process); NaHCO₃ (baking soda — baking powder, antacid, fire extinguishers); NaCl (food, preserving, raw material for Na, Cl₂ and NaOH).
**Uses of sodium:** coolant in some nuclear reactors (liquid Na conducts heat well), sodium-vapour street lamps (yellow light), making sodium compounds and reducing other metals (e.g. Ti from TiCl₄).

cards.title: Sodium reacts with water
body: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Sodium floats, melts into a ball and moves about; the solution becomes alkaline (turns red litmus blue).

cards.title: Worked: mass of sodium from a Downs cell
cards.problem: How many grams of sodium are produced at the cathode when 117 g of molten NaCl is completely electrolysed? (Na = 23, Cl = 35.5)

steps.text: Moles of NaCl = 117 ÷ 58.5 = 2.0 mol.
Cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na, so 1 mol NaCl gives 1 mol Na.
Mass of Na = 2.0 × 23 = 46 g (and 1.0 mol Cl₂ = 71 g at the anode).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why is CaCl₂ added to the NaCl in the Downs cell?

options.A: To lower the melting point of the electrolyte and save energy
options.D: To make the sodium heavier so it sinks

cards.why: Pure NaCl melts at about 801 °C. Adding CaCl₂ lowers the melting point to about 600 °C, so less energy is needed to keep the electrolyte molten.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Sodium is stored under paraffin oil because it:

options.A: Reacts quickly with oxygen and water vapour in air
options.B: Is a liquid at room temperature

cards.why: Sodium is very reactive: it tarnishes in air and reacts violently with water. Paraffin oil keeps air and moisture away and sodium does not react with it.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which sodium compound is used as baking powder and in some fire extinguishers?
cards.why: Sodium hydrogencarbonate (baking soda) decomposes on heating: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. The CO₂ makes dough rise and smothers fires.

cards.title: 4.3 Aluminium
body: **Occurrence:** the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust (about 8 %), found combined in clays and mainly in **bauxite, Al₂O₃·2H₂O**.
**Purification (Bayer process):** bauxite is dissolved in hot NaOH (Al₂O₃ is amphoteric), impurities such as Fe₂O₃ are filtered off, Al(OH)₃ is precipitated and heated to give pure alumina, Al₂O₃.

**Extraction (Hall–Héroult process):** alumina is dissolved in molten **cryolite (Na₃AlF₆)**, which lowers the working temperature to about 950 °C, and electrolysed with carbon electrodes. Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al. Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻; the oxygen burns the carbon anodes away (C + O₂ → CO₂), so they must be replaced regularly. The process uses a lot of electricity, so recycling aluminium saves energy.

**Properties:** light (density 2.7 g/cm³), good conductor of heat and electricity, malleable, ductile. Although reactive, it is protected by a thin, tough **oxide layer** (Al₂O₃) — this can be thickened by anodising. Amphoteric: reacts with acids and with alkalis.
**Uses:** overhead power cables, aircraft and vehicle bodies (as alloys such as duralumin), drink cans, cooking pots, foil, window frames. Alum, K₂SO₄·Al₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O, is used to purify water.

cards.title: Step by step: Aluminium
body: **Step 1:** Occurrence: most abundant metal in the Earth's crust (about 8 %); main ore bauxite Al₂O₃·2H₂O.
**Step 2:** Purification (Bayer process): bauxite is dissolved in hot NaOH, impurities (Fe₂O₃) are filtered off, Al(OH)₃ is precipitated and heated to pure Al₂O₃ (alumina).
**Step 3:** Extraction (Hall–Héroult): alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) to lower the melting point from about 2050 °C to about 950 °C, then electrolysed with carbon electrodes.
**Step 4:** Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al; anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻, and the oxygen burns the carbon anodes (so they are replaced regularly).
**Step 5:** Properties and uses: light, good conductor, resists corrosion because of a thin protective Al₂O₃ layer; amphoteric oxide. Used in power cables, aircraft, cans and window frames.
**Example:** Mass of Al from 102 kg of Al₂O₃: 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. M(Al₂O₃) = 102 g/mol, so 102 kg = 1000 mol Al₂O₃ → 2000 mol Al × 27 g/mol = 54 kg of aluminium.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Bayer Purifies, Hall Electrolyses, Cryolite Cools"
body: B-P, H-E, C-C.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Explain why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis, not carbon: it is above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot reduce Al₂O₃.

cards.title: Worked: aluminium from alumina
cards.problem: What mass of aluminium can be obtained from 204 t of pure alumina, Al₂O₃? (Al = 27, O = 16)

steps.text: Molar mass Al₂O₃ = 2(27) + 3(16) = 102.
Each Al₂O₃ contains 2 Al, so mass fraction of Al = 54/102.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why is alumina dissolved in molten cryolite before electrolysis?

options.A: To lower the operating temperature and save energy
options.B: To make aluminium react faster with oxygen
options.C: Because cryolite is the ore of aluminium

cards.why: Alumina melts above 2000 °C. Dissolved in molten cryolite it can be electrolysed at about 950 °C, which saves a great deal of energy.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The carbon anodes in aluminium extraction must be replaced regularly because:

options.A: Oxygen formed at the anode burns them to CO₂

cards.why: Oxide ions are discharged at the anode as O₂; at that temperature the oxygen reacts with the carbon to form CO₂, so the anodes wear away.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Aluminium is high in the reactivity series, yet aluminium pots do not corrode in air. Why?

options.A: A thin, unreactive layer of Al₂O₃ protects the surface
options.B: Aluminium does not react with oxygen

cards.why: Aluminium reacts with air at once to form a thin, tough, non-porous Al₂O₃ layer that sticks to the metal and stops further attack.

cards.title: Five important metals at a glance
head: Metal
Remember
rows: Bauxite → electrolysis of Al₂O₃ in cryolite. Light, oxide skin stops further rust. Cans, planes, cables.
Haematite in the blast furnace with coke + limestone. Steel = Fe + C (+ other). Rusts unless protected.
Excellent conductor, unreactive enough for pipes and wires. Electro-refining.
Galvanising — sacrificial protection of iron. Also brass (Cu+Zn).
Native, very unreactive, jewellery and electronics. Soft — often alloyed.

cards.title: 4.4 Iron — extraction and steel
body: **Ores:** haematite (Fe₂O₃), magnetite (Fe₃O₄), limonite (2Fe₂O₃·3H₂O), siderite (FeCO₃) and iron pyrites (FeS₂ — not used for iron because of the sulphur).
**Blast furnace:** iron ore, coke and limestone go in at the top; hot air is blown in at the bottom.
1. Coke burns: C + O₂ → CO₂ (gives heat). 2. CO₂ + C → 2CO. 3. CO reduces the ore: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.
4. Limestone removes sand (the main impurity): CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (**slag**). Molten slag floats on the molten iron and both are tapped off.

**Pig/cast iron** (about 4 % C) is hard but brittle. **Steel** is made by blowing oxygen through molten iron to burn off most of the carbon, then adding controlled amounts of C, Cr, Ni, Mn etc. Mild steel (≈0.25 % C) — car bodies, nails; stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni) — cutlery, sinks.

**Rusting** needs both water and oxygen: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 2xH₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Prevented by painting, oiling, plastic coating, galvanising (zinc), tin-plating or sacrificial blocks of a more reactive metal.

cards.title: Worked: iron from haematite
cards.problem: Calculate the mass of iron that can be obtained from 480 kg of haematite, Fe₂O₃. (Fe = 56, O = 16)

steps.text: Molar mass Fe₂O₃ = 2(56) + 3(16) = 160.
Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂: 160 kg of ore gives 112 kg of iron.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the main reducing agent for iron oxide in the blast furnace?
cards.why: Coke burns to CO₂, which reacts with more coke to give CO. Carbon monoxide removes oxygen from the ore: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Limestone is added to the blast furnace in order to:

options.C: Raise the carbon content of the iron

cards.why: Limestone decomposes to CaO, a basic oxide, which reacts with acidic SiO₂ (sand) to form calcium silicate slag: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Galvanised iron does not rust even when scratched because:

options.A: Zinc is more reactive and corrodes in place of the iron
options.B: Zinc is less reactive than iron

cards.why: Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series, so it loses electrons in preference to iron (sacrificial protection), even where the coating is broken.

cards.title: Worked: rust conditions
cards.problem: Does iron rust in dry pure oxygen alone easily?

steps.text: Rusting needs both water and oxygen typically.

cards.answer: Moisture is required for ordinary rusting.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In a Blast Furnace, the primary chemical species acting as the reducing agent to convert iron ore to metallic iron is:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze Blast Furnace gas reactions**
Coke ($$C$$) burns to form $$CO_2$$, which reacts with excess coke to form carbon monoxide ($$CO$$).

**Step 2: Identify the active reducing agent**
While carbon (coke) is the original source, it is carbon monoxide ($$CO$$) gas that actually diffuses upwards and reduces the hematite ($$Fe_2O_3$$) solid to liquid iron.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct option is **B**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Stainless steel resists rusting because it contains:
cards.why: Chromium forms a thin protective oxide layer on the surface of stainless steel, which stops oxygen and water reaching the iron.

cards.title: 4.5 Copper
body: **Ores:** chalcopyrite (copper pyrites, CuFeS₂ — the main ore), chalcocite (Cu₂S), cuprite (Cu₂O) and malachite (CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂). Eritrea's Bisha and Debarwa deposits contain copper sulphide ores.

**Extraction from sulphide ore:** 1) the ore is crushed and concentrated by **froth flotation**; 2) it is **roasted** in air: 2CuFeS₂ + 4O₂ → Cu₂S + 2FeO + 3SO₂; 3) iron is removed as slag (FeO + SiO₂ → FeSiO₃); 4) Cu₂S is partly oxidised and the oxide reacts with the remaining sulphide (**self-reduction**): 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S → 6Cu + SO₂. This gives impure **blister copper** (about 98 %).

**Electrolytic refining:** impure copper is the **anode**, a thin strip of pure copper the **cathode**, and acidified CuSO₄ solution the electrolyte. Anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (99.98 % pure). Impurities such as Ag and Au fall as **anode sludge**.

**Properties:** reddish-brown, excellent conductor of electricity and heat, ductile, malleable, does not react with dilute HCl or H₂SO₄ (below hydrogen). In moist air it slowly forms a green coating (basic copper carbonate).
**Uses:** electric wires and cables, water pipes, cooking vessels, coins; alloys brass (Cu + Zn) and bronze (Cu + Sn). CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue vitriol) is used as a fungicide (Bordeaux mixture).

cards.title: Worked: refining copper
cards.problem: During electrolytic refining, the anode loses 12.8 g of copper. What mass of copper is deposited on the cathode, and how many moles of electrons flowed? (Cu = 64)

steps.text: Anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻; cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu — copper simply moves from anode to cathode.
Mass deposited = 12.8 g (ignoring impurities).
Moles Cu = 12.8 ÷ 64 = 0.20 mol; electrons = 2 × 0.20 = 0.40 mol.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In the electrolytic refining of copper, the impure copper is made the:
cards.why: Copper atoms of the impure anode go into solution as Cu²⁺ and are deposited as pure copper on the cathode; impurities fall to the bottom as anode sludge.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which process concentrates a copper sulphide ore by making the ore particles stick to air bubbles?
cards.why: In froth flotation the powdered ore is mixed with water, oil and air. Sulphide particles are wetted by the oil, cling to the froth and are skimmed off; the gangue sinks.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Copper is used for electrical wiring mainly because it:

options.A: Is a very good conductor and is ductile
options.D: Reacts with water to give hydrogen

cards.why: Copper has very high electrical conductivity (second only to silver), can be drawn into wires and resists corrosion.

cards.title: 4.6 Zinc
body: **Ores:** zinc blende (sphalerite, ZnS — the main ore), calamine (ZnCO₃) and zincite (ZnO). Zinc is also produced at Eritrea's Bisha mine.

**Extraction:** the ore is concentrated by froth flotation, then converted to the oxide — ZnS by **roasting**: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂ (the SO₂ is used to make sulphuric acid); ZnCO₃ by **calcination**: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂.

The oxide is reduced with coke at about 1400 °C: ZnO + C → Zn + CO. Zinc boils at 907 °C, so it distils off as vapour and is condensed. Alternatively ZnO is dissolved in H₂SO₄ and the ZnSO₄ solution is **electrolysed** to give very pure zinc.
**Properties:** bluish-white, fairly reactive (above iron, below aluminium), amphoteric oxide; reacts with dilute acids to give H₂: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.
**Uses:** galvanising iron (roofing sheets), the casing of dry cells, brass (Cu + Zn), die-casting alloys; ZnO in paints, ointments and rubber.

cards.title: Step by step: Zinc
body: **Step 1:** Ores: zinc blende (ZnS, main ore), calamine (ZnCO₃) and zincite (ZnO); zinc is also produced at Eritrea's Bisha mine.
**Step 2:** Concentrate the ore by froth flotation, then roast in air: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂ (the SO₂ can be used to make sulphuric acid).
**Step 3:** Reduce the oxide with carbon (coke) in a furnace: ZnO + C → Zn + CO; zinc vapour is condensed – or dissolve ZnO in H₂SO₄ and electrolyse the ZnSO₄ solution (purer zinc).
**Step 4:** Properties: bluish-white metal, fairly reactive, reacts with dilute acids to give H₂; ZnO and Zn(OH)₂ are amphoteric.
**Step 5:** Uses: galvanizing iron (sacrificial protection), brass (Cu + Zn), dry-cell cases, ZnO in paints and creams.
**Example:** Galvanized iron sheets on Eritrean roofs: even when scratched, zinc corrodes first because it is more reactive than iron, so the iron underneath stays protected (sacrificial protection).

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Float, Roast, Reduce"
body: F-R-R turns zinc blende into zinc.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: For any sulphide ore remember: first roast to the oxide (releasing SO₂), then reduce the oxide. Write both equations.

cards.title: Worked: SO₂ from roasting zinc blende
cards.problem: What volume of SO₂ at STP is produced when 194 kg of ZnS is roasted? (Zn = 65, S = 32; molar volume 22.4 L)

steps.text: Molar mass ZnS = 97 g/mol, so 194 kg = 194 000 ÷ 97 = 2000 mol.
2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂: 1 mol ZnS gives 1 mol SO₂ → 2000 mol SO₂.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Zinc blende must be roasted before reduction with carbon because:

options.A: Carbon reduces oxides, so the sulphide must first be changed to ZnO

cards.why: Carbon cannot easily reduce sulphides. Roasting in air converts ZnS into ZnO, which coke then reduces: ZnO + C → Zn + CO.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In the carbon-reduction method, zinc is collected by condensing its vapour. This is possible because zinc:

options.B: Is a gas at room temperature

cards.why: The furnace is hotter than 907 °C, so zinc forms as a vapour that is led away and condensed.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Brass is an alloy of zinc with:
cards.why: Brass is copper + zinc. Bronze is copper + tin.

cards.title: 4.7 Gold
body: **Occurrence:** gold is so unreactive that it occurs **native** (as the free metal) — as grains in quartz veins and in river sands (placer deposits). Eritrea has gold at Bisha, Koka, Zara and in the ancient workings of the Asmara area.

**Extraction:** placer gold can be separated by **panning/washing** because gold is very dense (19.3 g/cm³). Gold in rock is crushed and dissolved by **cyanidation**: 4Au + 8NaCN + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4Na[Au(CN)₂] + 4NaOH. The gold is then displaced by zinc: 2Na[Au(CN)₂] + Zn → Na₂[Zn(CN)₄] + 2Au, and refined by electrolysis. (Cyanide is very poisonous, so mine waste must be handled carefully.)
**Properties:** yellow, very dense, the most malleable and ductile metal, excellent conductor, does not tarnish or react with ordinary acids; dissolves only in **aqua regia** (3 HCl : 1 HNO₃).
**Purity:** measured in **carats** — pure gold is 24 carat; 18-carat gold is 18/24 = 75 % gold alloyed with copper or silver to make it harder.
**Uses:** jewellery, coins and national reserves, electronic contacts, dentistry, reflective coatings.

cards.title: Step by step: Gold
body: **Step 1:** Gold is very unreactive (at the bottom of the reactivity series), so it occurs native as free metal in quartz veins and river sands; Eritrea has gold mining at Bisha and Zara and an ancient tradition of panning.
**Step 2:** Concentration: crushed ore or sand is washed (panning) because gold is very dense (19.3 g/cm³).
**Step 3:** Cyanide process: gold dissolves in sodium cyanide solution in the presence of air, forming the soluble complex [Au(CN)₂]⁻.
**Step 4:** Recovery: zinc (or activated carbon then electrolysis) displaces gold from the solution: 2[Au(CN)₂]⁻ + Zn → [Zn(CN)₄]²⁻ + 2Au.

**Step 5:** Properties and uses: shiny, does not tarnish, most malleable and ductile metal, good conductor; used in jewellery, electronics, dentistry and as a reserve of wealth. Purity is measured in carats (24 carat = pure).
**Example:** An 18-carat ring contains 18/24 = 75 % gold; the other 25 % is usually copper and silver to make it harder.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Native, Dense, Cyanide, Zinc"
body: N-D-C-Z: occurs free, washed by density, dissolved by cyanide, recovered by zinc.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Gold dissolves in aqua regia (3 HCl : 1 HNO₃) but not in a single ordinary acid – a common exam question.

cards.title: Worked: carats
cards.problem: A ring of mass 8.0 g is made of 18-carat gold. What mass of pure gold does it contain?

steps.text: Pure gold = 24 carat, so 18 carat means 18/24 of the mass is gold.
Mass of gold = 0.75 × 8.0 = 6.0 g (the other 2.0 g is mostly copper or silver).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Gold is found as the free metal in nature mainly because it:
cards.why: Gold is at the bottom of the reactivity series; it does not react with oxygen, water or most acids, so it stays uncombined (native).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which mixture dissolves gold?
cards.why: Nitric acid oxidises gold slightly and chloride ions remove Au³⁺ as [AuCl₄]⁻, so the mixture dissolves gold although neither acid does alone.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Panning separates gold from river sand because gold:
cards.why: Gold (19.3 g/cm³) is about seven times denser than sand, so swirling with water washes the light sand away and leaves gold in the pan.

cards.title: 4.8 Alloys
body: An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually metals, sometimes carbon). Atoms of different sizes disturb the regular layers of the metal lattice, so layers cannot slide easily: alloys are usually **harder and stronger** than the pure metal, may resist corrosion better and often have a lower melting point.

Brass (Cu + Zn) — taps, musical instruments, ornaments. Bronze (Cu + Sn) — statues, medals, bells. Steel (Fe + C) and stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni) — construction, cutlery. Duralumin (Al + Cu + Mg + Mn) — aircraft bodies. Solder (Sn + Pb) — joining wires, low melting point. Amalgam (Hg + another metal) — dental fillings. 18-carat gold (Au + Cu/Ag) — jewellery.

cards.title: Step by step: Alloys
body: **Step 1:** An alloy is a mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually metals, sometimes carbon), made by melting them together.
**Step 2:** Atoms of different sizes disturb the regular layers of the metal lattice, so the layers cannot slide easily – the alloy is harder and stronger than the pure metal.
**Step 3:** Alloys may also resist corrosion better or have a lower melting point.
**Step 4:** Common alloys: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn), steel (Fe + C), stainless steel (Fe + Cr + Ni), solder (Sn + Pb), duralumin (Al + Cu + Mg).
**Step 5:** Choose the alloy by the property needed: strength, corrosion resistance, low melting point or appearance.
**Example:** Pure aluminium is soft; duralumin (about 95 % Al with Cu, Mg, Mn) stays light but is much stronger, so it is used for aircraft bodies.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Brass has Zinc, Bronze has Tin"
body: Bra-Z, Bro-T.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: In "why are alloys harder?" questions draw two diagrams: neat rows of identical atoms (layers slide) vs rows disturbed by bigger/smaller atoms (layers cannot slide).

cards.title: Worked: composition of an alloy
cards.problem: A 250 g bronze bell contains 88 % copper and the rest tin. Find the masses of copper and tin.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why are alloys usually harder than the pure metals they are made from?

options.A: Different-sized atoms stop the layers of atoms sliding over each other
options.C: Alloys are compounds with fixed formulas

cards.why: In a pure metal, identical atoms form regular layers that slide easily. Atoms of another size distort the layers and make sliding harder.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which alloy is used for aircraft bodies because it is light and strong?
cards.why: Duralumin is mainly aluminium (light) with small amounts of copper, magnesium and manganese, which make it much stronger than pure aluminium.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Brass is an alloy of:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Brass = copper + zinc.

**Step 2:** Bronze = copper + tin; steel = iron + carbon; solder = tin + lead.

**Step 3:** Answer: copper and zinc.

**Tip:** "Brass has Zinc, Bronze has Tin."

similar.q: The impurities from an ore can be removed by  A) treating the ore with an acid.  B) reducing the ore on heating strongly.  C) treating the ore with cold water.  D) heating the ore in air.  E) A and B.
similar.a: A. treating the ore with an acid.

questions.q: The impurities from an ore can be removed by

options.A: treating the ore with an acid.
options.B: reducing the ore on heating strongly.
options.C: treating the ore with cold water.

why: The impurities (gangue: soil, sand) are removed by physical or chemical methods that exploit differences between gangue and ore.

units.title: Behaviour of Gases
units.intro: Gases fill the container, are easy to compress, mix, and their pressure comes from wall hits.

cards.title: 5.1 The gaseous state
body: Gas particles are far apart and move rapidly and randomly, so gases **have no fixed shape or volume**, are easily **compressed**, **expand** to fill their container, have **low density** and **diffuse** quickly into each other.

A gas sample is described by four measurable quantities: **pressure P** (Pa, kPa, atm, mmHg; 1 atm = 101.3 kPa = 760 mmHg), **volume V** (m³, L, cm³; 1 L = 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³), **temperature T** (always in kelvin for gas calculations: T = t °C + 273) and **amount n** (mol).
**Pressure** is caused by gas particles hitting the walls of the container; it is measured with a barometer (atmospheric pressure) or a manometer (gas in a container).
**STP** (standard temperature and pressure) = 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atm (101.3 kPa). At STP one mole of any ideal gas occupies about **22.4 L**.

cards.title: Quick check

**Step 1: Recall the definition of Boyle's Law**
Boyle's Law state that at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.

**Step 2: Identify variables**

**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: The gaseous state
body: A gas is described by pressure P, volume V, temperature T and amount n.
T(K) = t(C) + 273. Never use Celsius in Charles or PV = nRT.

cards.title: Step by step: The gaseous state
body: **Step 1:** Gas particles are far apart and move fast and randomly, so gases have no fixed shape or volume, are easily compressed and fill their container.
**Step 2:** A gas sample is described by four variables: pressure P (Pa, kPa, atm, mmHg), volume V (L, m³), temperature T (kelvin) and amount n (mol).
**Step 3:** Convert temperature: T(K) = t(°C) + 273. Standard temperature and pressure (STP): 273 K and 1 atm (101.3 kPa); 1 mol of ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at STP.
**Step 4:** Pressure units: 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 101.3 kPa.
**Step 5:** Gases diffuse: lighter gases diffuse faster (Graham's law: rate ∝ 1/√M).
**Example:** How many moles are in 11.2 L of O₂ at STP? n = 11.2 L ÷ 22.4 L/mol = 0.50 mol, mass = 0.50 × 32 = 16 g.

cards.title: 5.2 The gas laws
body: **Boyle's law:** at constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ (a graph of P against 1/V is a straight line through the origin).

**Charles' law:** at constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its kelvin temperature: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. Extending the V–t graph to V = 0 gives **absolute zero, −273 °C (0 K)**.
**Gay-Lussac's (pressure) law:** at constant volume, P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂. **Combined gas law:** P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
**Avogadro's law:** equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules (V ∝ n).
**Ideal gas equation:** PV = nRT, with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (P in Pa, V in m³) or 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Using n = m/M it also gives molar mass: M = mRT/(PV), and density d = PM/(RT).

**Dalton's law of partial pressures:** the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures: P_total = P₁ + P₂ + … . **Graham's law:** rate of diffusion ∝ 1/√M, so light gases (H₂, He) diffuse fastest.

cards.title: Deriving the ideal gas equation, step by step
body: Four variables describe a gas: pressure **P**, volume **V**, temperature **T** (kelvin) and amount **n** (mol). Each gas law links V to one of the others while the rest are kept fixed:
**Step 1 — Boyle (n, T fixed):** \(V \propto \dfrac{1}{P}\)
**Step 2 — Charles (n, P fixed):** \(V \propto T\)
**Step 3 — Avogadro (P, T fixed):** \(V \propto n\)
**Step 4 — Combine:** if V is proportional to each separately, it is proportional to all together: \(V \propto \dfrac{nT}{P}\).
**Step 5 — Put in a constant R** (the molar gas constant): \(V = R\,\dfrac{nT}{P}\), so
$$PV = nRT$$

**Step 6 — Find R** from one known gas: 1 mol at STP (273 K, 1 atm) occupies 22.4 L, so \(R = \dfrac{PV}{nT} = \dfrac{1 \times 22.4}{1 \times 273} = 0.0821\ \text{L}\cdot\text{atm/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}\). In SI units (P in Pa, V in m³): R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
**Check:** fix n and T → PV = constant (Boyle); fix n and P → V/T = constant (Charles); fix n → PV/T = constant (combined gas law).

steps.text: **Boyle:** V ∝ 1/P when n and T are fixed.
**Charles:** V ∝ T when n and P are fixed.
**Avogadro:** V ∝ n when P and T are fixed.
Put the three together: **V ∝ nT/P**.
Replace “∝” by “= R ×”: **PV = nRT**.
Substitute n = m/M and d = m/V: **PM = dRT**.

cards.title: PM = dRT: density and molar mass of a gas
body: **Step 1:** moles = mass ÷ molar mass: \(n = \dfrac{m}{M}\).
**Step 2:** substitute into PV = nRT: \(PV = \dfrac{m}{M}RT\).
**Step 3:** multiply both sides by M and divide by V: \(PM = \dfrac{m}{V}RT\).
**Step 4:** m/V is the density d:
$$PM = dRT \qquad d = \frac{PM}{RT} \qquad M = \frac{dRT}{P}$$

**What it tells you:** at the same P and T, a gas with a bigger molar mass is denser (CO₂, M = 44, sinks below air, M ≈ 29; H₂ and He rise). Heating a gas lowers its density (hot-air balloons). Measuring the density of an unknown gas gives its molar mass.

steps.text: \(V = \dfrac{nRT}{P} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 0.0821 \times 300}{2.0}\)

steps.text: Use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), so V must be in m³: 10.0 L = 0.0100 m³.
\(P = \dfrac{nRT}{V} = \dfrac{0.50 \times 8.314 \times 300}{0.0100}\)
\(P = 1.25\times10^{5}\text{ Pa}\) (about 1.23 atm)

cards.title: Worked example: density of CO₂ at STP
cards.problem: Calculate the density of carbon dioxide (M = 44 g/mol) at STP.

steps.text: \(d = \dfrac{PM}{RT} = \dfrac{1 \times 44}{0.0821 \times 273}\)

cards.title: Worked example: molar mass from density

steps.text: \(M = \dfrac{dRT}{P} = \dfrac{1.25 \times 0.0821 \times 273}{1}\)
M = 28.0 g/mol
Gases with M = 28: N₂ or CO (or C₂H₄).

cards.title: The Kinetic Molecular Theory of Gases
body: **Kinetic theory:** tiny particles, random motion, elastic hits, T is average KE. Ideal gas = no attraction, point masses.

cards.title: Real gases and the van der Waals equation, step by step
body: **Ideal gas assumptions (kinetic theory):** (1) the molecules themselves take up **no volume**; (2) there are **no attractions** between molecules. Real gases obey PV = nRT well only at **low pressure and high temperature**.
**Step 1 — Why real gases deviate.** At **high pressure** the molecules are crowded, so their own volume is no longer negligible. At **low temperature** they move slowly, so attractions matter.
**Step 2 — Volume correction.** Each mole of molecules occupies a volume b, so the empty space molecules can move in is the **free volume** V − nb.

**Step 3 — Pressure correction.** A molecule about to hit the wall is pulled back by its neighbours, so it hits more gently: the measured P is **less** than the ideal pressure. The loss depends on how crowded the gas is, \((n/V)^2\), so we add \(\dfrac{an^2}{V^2}\).
**Step 4 — Put both into PV = nRT** (textbook 5.3.3, Van der Waals’ equation):
$$\left(P + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT$$

**Meaning of the constants:** **a** measures the strength of attractions (large for polar or big molecules that are easy to liquefy, e.g. NH₃, H₂O); **b** measures the size of the molecules. The smaller a and b, the more ideal the gas (He and H₂ are closest to ideal).

states.label: Ideal
states.text: Ideal model: molecules are points with no attractions — PV = nRT.

states.label: Volume
states.text: Real molecules take up space: the free volume is V − nb. This matters most at high pressure.

states.label: Pressure
states.text: Neighbours pull a molecule back as it reaches the wall, so the wall feels less pressure: add an²/V². This matters most at low temperature.

(b) Rearrange: \(P = \dfrac{nRT}{V - nb} - \dfrac{an^2}{V^2}\)
The real pressure is about 10 % lower: the attraction effect is bigger than the volume effect here.

cards.title: Worked example: when is a gas most ideal?

steps.text: **Low pressure:** molecules are far apart, so nb is tiny compared with V and an²/V² is tiny compared with P.
**High temperature:** molecules move fast, so brief attractions hardly slow them — the pressure correction is unimportant.
So: **low pressure and high temperature**, and gases with small a and b (He, H₂).

cards.title: Step by step: Kinetic molecular theory and the gas laws
body: **Step 1:** Postulates: gas particles are tiny compared with the distances between them; they move randomly in straight lines; collisions are perfectly elastic; there are no attractive forces; average kinetic energy ∝ absolute temperature.
**Step 2:** Boyle's law (T, n constant): P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ – squeezing particles into less space makes more collisions with the walls.
**Step 3:** Charles's law (P, n constant): V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ – hotter particles move faster and push the walls out.
**Step 4:** Combined and ideal gas laws: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ and PV = nRT (R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) = 8.314 J/(mol·K)).
**Step 5:** Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature, because particles then have volume and attract each other.
**Example:** A gas occupies 2.0 L at 27 °C. Volume at 127 °C (same P)? T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 400 K. V₂ = V₁ × T₂/T₁ = 2.0 × 400/300 = 2.67 L.

cards.q: Absolute zero, the theoretical point of zero molecular volume and motion, is mathematically defined as:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define Absolute Zero**
Absolute zero is the zero point on the Kelvin scale ($$0\text{ K}$$).

**Step 2: Convert to Celsius scale**
$$T(\text{K}) = T(^\circ\text{C}) + 273.15 \implies 0 = T(^\circ\text{C}) + 273.15 \implies T(^\circ\text{C}) = -273.15^\circ\text{C}$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
Absolute zero is **$$-273.15^\circ\text{C}$$**, option **B**.

questions.q: A gas exerts a pressure of 1.5 atm on a 5.0 L container at 27 °C and has a density of 1.06 g/L. The molecular mass of the gas is [Ideal gas constant (R) = 0.082 L.atm/mol.K]
why:
**Step 1:** Convert Temp to Kelvin: $$27 + 273 = 300\text{ K}$$.
**Step 2:** Use the Ideal Gas Law formula involving density ($$\rho$$): $$M = (\rho RT) / P$$.
**Step 3:** $$M = (1.06 \times 0.082 \times 300) / 1.5$$
**Step 4:** $$M = (1.06 \times 24.6) / 1.5 = 26.076 / 1.5 = 17.384\text{ g/mol}$$.

questions.q: A given mass of gas occupies a volume of 500cc at a pressure P absolute temperature T. What will its volume be when the temperature and pressure doubled?
why:
**Step 1: Use the Combined Gas Law.**
$$ \frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2} $$

**Step 2: Substitute the new conditions.**
- $$ P_2 = 2P_1 $$
- $$ T_2 = 2T_1 $$
- $$ V_1 = 500cc $$

**Step 3: Solve for $$ V_2 $$.**
$$ \frac{P_1 \times 500}{T_1} = \frac{2P_1 \times V_2}{2T_1} $$
$$ \frac{P_1 \times 500}{T_1} = \frac{P_1 \times V_2}{T_1} $$
$$ V_2 = 500cc $$.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Which of the following relationships of gases is stated by Boyle’s Law?

options.B: $$ V \propto n $$ (at constant P and T)
options.C: $$ V \propto T $$ (at constant n and P)
options.D: $$ P \propto T $$ (at constant m and V)
options.E: $$ V \propto P $$ (at constant n and T)

why:
**Boyle's Law** states that for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the volume ($$ V $$) is inversely proportional to the pressure ($$ P $$). 
Formula: $$ P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 $$ or $$ V \propto 1/P $$.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

Step 3: Avogadro V ∝ n.
Step 4: together V ∝ nT/P → PV = nRT.
